title: Tesla Cybercab Launch Event — Austin, 2026 | MyCybercab.com
excerpt: Two seats. Butterfly doors. Zero steering wheel. Everything from Tesla's Austin Cybercab launch — footage, specs, fares, sightings, and the storm after.
content_html:
MYCYBERCAB.COM

Two seats. Butterfly doors. Zero steering wheel. Everything from Tesla's Austin Cybercab launch — footage, specs, fares, sightings, and the storm after.

Sept 3, 2026

ACL Live, Austin

No wheel · No pedals

Public rides: limited Austin

Cybercab launch event presentation:

At the Austin launch, Tesla's engineering and design leads unveiled the finished Cybercab and confirmed the fleet has now passed one million miles of unsupervised robotaxi operation, calling it the result of 12 years of self-driving development. They detailed the car's camera-only, AI-first driving stack, its accessibility features built with disability groups and first responders, and a "second living room" cabin experience with Grok voice integration and app-based personalization.

The safest car on the road, according to Tesla

Tesla's own promo built around the Cybercab makes one claim front and center: this is designed to be the safest vehicle they've ever put on the road. No driver error possible, no distracted human behind the wheel, because there's no wheel to be distracted from.

Brake-by-wire, no brake fluid

Cybercab is the first Tesla to ship with a fully electronic brake-by-wire system — no hydraulic brake fluid line at all. Every other Tesla on the road today still runs a traditional hydraulic brake circuit as a backup layer. Cybercab replaces it entirely with electronic actuation, lighter and with fewer points of failure over the vehicle's life.

A sound system built for the cabin, and lights that move with it

Tesla engineered a purpose-built audio system for the Cybercab's two-seat cabin rather than adapting a system from an existing model. The ambient interior lighting is tied directly to the music — the light bar and cabin accents pulse and shift in sync with whatever's playing.

The interface was built in Unreal Engine

Cybercab's in-cabin display and interaction design were built using Epic Games' Unreal Engine — the same real-time 3D engine behind major video game titles — rather than a typical automotive UI toolkit.

What's actually running the show

Under the skin, Cybercab runs on Tesla's latest compute hardware — the same processing backbone driving FSD across the fleet, tuned for a car that has to make every driving decision itself with no human fallback.

A thermal system that's 80% automated to build

Cybercab is the first Tesla to use the company's next-generation Supermanifold V3 thermal system — a redesign that strips out unnecessary refrigerant valves and lines and consolidates the high- and low-voltage controllers into a single module.

"We removed unnecessary refrigerant valves and lines and consolidated the high- and low-voltage controllers, reducing parts and complexity. Its modular design makes its production 80% automated and its operation 38% more efficient than other automotive thermal systems."

Proper Props

While the attendees & patrons were filing into the Launch Event, hours before the start time, Jaan @theevuniverse & Simon @residentsponge from EVWire already had the Inside Scope. Jaan put out an 8 part X thread breaking down all of the latest NEWS 1st!

Jaan & Simon from EVwire are a Must Follow, they cover All EV from ALL angles for the entire industry, 1st to the news & Setting the Standard.

Safety and federal compliance, straight from Tesla's own filing

Tesla publishes a formal compliance guide for Cybercab covering how the vehicle meets Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards despite having no steering wheel or pedals — the exact regulatory territory NHTSA has been actively rewriting rules around this year.

Read the full compliance guide (PDF) →

Tesla is already signing up fleet operators

Beyond individual riders, Tesla is actively building out a network of fleet operators and partners to scale the Robotaxi service. If you're exploring what it takes to operate or invest in a Cybercab fleet, Tesla has an official interest form live now.

Register fleet interest with Tesla →

What actually happens during a ride

After your ride ends, Tesla uses the interior cabin camera to confirm the Cybercab is ready for its next passenger, checking whether the cabin is clean and whether anything was left behind. A green light turns on any time the camera is actively recording, so you always know when it's on. Riders can also adjust interior ambient lighting colors directly from the Tesla app — @TheEvUniverse — EVWire

Photo: Jaan @ EVWire

Photo: Jaan @ EVWire

Eight cameras, and seatbelts that talk to you

Cybercab is covered by eight external and internal cameras feeding its self-driving and cabin-monitoring systems continuously.

The motorized seatbelts do more than tighten automatically. They can pulse or vibrate to get a passenger's attention, and they proactively tighten the moment the car anticipates or detects harsh braking, loss of traction, or another sudden road event.

⚠ Important: don't ride with your feet up on the dash. Airbag deployment paths assume feet are on the floor.

Not yet built for young kids

Children under 13 are not currently permitted in a Cybercab — even accompanied by an adult. Expect this to be one of the more actively revisited restrictions as Tesla expands the service.

Built with accessibility in mind, down to the door panel

Braille appears throughout the Cybercab cabin, including on interior touch points and controls — spelling out "CYBERCAB" here the same way it's marked in the car. For riders who are blind or have low vision, and for passengers with a range of physical disabilities, this is one of the small but deliberate details that make an unsupervised, driverless ride feel usable rather than just automated.

Price, Cybercab Vs Uber $

@niccruzpatane on X — a Must Follow! Tesla Cybercab vs Uber pricing in Austin, TX for a 2.17 mile route.

Cybercab: $6.42 ($2.95 per mile)
UberX (before tip): $11.95 ($5.50 per mile)

Out_Of_Spec Review a Quick Walk around

The legend Kyle Conner @itskyleconner with a Very high level Look underneath The Cybercab, A Nerd Video.

Exit safely

The final screen prompt before you step out — a simple, deliberate reminder that closes out every ride.

Video: @DavidMoss / X

This page will keep updating as the Austin fleet grows. Next up on MyCybercab.com: live day-one ride pricing on /prices, and real rider writeups on /reviews — both launching in the days following the event. Every sighting logged by the community continues to feed our live map in real time.

Common questions

Is Cybercab available to the public in Austin right now?

Yes, in a limited service area following the September 3, 2026 launch event. It's rolling out alongside Tesla's existing Model Y Robotaxi fleet, not replacing it yet.

Does Cybercab really have no steering wheel or pedals?

Correct — no manual controls of any kind. It's built exclusively for unsupervised autonomous operation.

What's the real range — 418 miles or 300?

418 miles is the EPA-equivalent all-electric rating (375 highway). Tesla has publicly cited approximately 300 miles as the more realistic real-world figure.

Is $0.20 per mile what I'll actually pay today?

No — that's Tesla's long-term operating-cost target once the fleet scales, not a current fare. Actual day-one pricing is tracked on our /prices page.

How is Cybercab different from the Model Y Robotaxi already running in Austin?

Same app, same service — different vehicle. Model Y Robotaxi is a standard production Model Y running Tesla's autonomy stack. Cybercab is purpose-built from the ground up with no manual controls at all.

Can Cybercab carry two people and luggage?

It's a two-seat vehicle with a front trunk for storage. It is not designed for wheelchair accessibility in its current configuration.

How we got here

Feb 17, 2026

First production Cybercab rolls off the line at Gigafactory Texas.

April 2026

Continuous production confirmed at scale.

June 2026

Engineering test rides begin on Austin public roads.

August 2026

Texas commercial registrations filed; official sweepstakes opens for launch event access.

Sept 3, 2026

Launch event at ACL Live, Austin. Limited public rides begin the same night.

Spotted a Cybercab?

Add it to the map and help the community track exactly where the fleet is showing up.

MrJavierJose

@mrjavierjose · San Jose, CA · hello@mycybercab.com

Founder of MyCybercab.com, a community-run Tesla Cybercab sighting tracker. Also runs TeslaSemi.com. Tracking the Cybercab rollout since the first production unit left the factory floor.

Information on this page is compiled from public sources, official Tesla materials, and community submissions, and may change as Tesla updates its Robotaxi and Cybercab program.

content_html_zh:
MYCYBERCAB.COM

Two seats. Butterfly doors. Zero steering wheel. Everything from Tesla's Austin Cybercab launch — footage, specs, fares, sightings, and the storm after.

Sept 3, 2026

ACL Live, Austin

No wheel · No pedals

Public rides: limited Austin

Cybercab launch event presentation:

At the Austin launch, Tesla's engineering and design leads unveiled the finished Cybercab and confirmed the fleet has now passed one million miles of unsupervised robotaxi operation, calling it the result of 12 years of self-driving development. They detailed the car's camera-only, AI-first driving stack, its accessibility features built with disability groups and first responders, and a "second living room" cabin experience with Grok voice integration and app-based personalization.

The safest car on the road, according to Tesla

Tesla's own promo built around the Cybercab makes one claim front and center: this is designed to be the safest vehicle they've ever put on the road. No driver error possible, no distracted human behind the wheel, because there's no wheel to be distracted from.

Brake-by-wire, no brake fluid

Cybercab is the first Tesla to ship with a fully electronic brake-by-wire system — no hydraulic brake fluid line at all. Every other Tesla on the road today still runs a traditional hydraulic brake circuit as a backup layer. Cybercab replaces it entirely with electronic actuation, lighter and with fewer points of failure over the vehicle's life.

A sound system built for the cabin, and lights that move with it

Tesla engineered a purpose-built audio system for the Cybercab's two-seat cabin rather than adapting a system from an existing model. The ambient interior lighting is tied directly to the music — the light bar and cabin accents pulse and shift in sync with whatever's playing.

The interface was built in Unreal Engine

Cybercab's in-cabin display and interaction design were built using Epic Games' Unreal Engine — the same real-time 3D engine behind major video game titles — rather than a typical automotive UI toolkit.

What's actually running the show

Under the skin, Cybercab runs on Tesla's latest compute hardware — the same processing backbone driving FSD across the fleet, tuned for a car that has to make every driving decision itself with no human fallback.

A thermal system that's 80% automated to build

Cybercab is the first Tesla to use the company's next-generation Supermanifold V3 thermal system — a redesign that strips out unnecessary refrigerant valves and lines and consolidates the high- and low-voltage controllers into a single module.

"We removed unnecessary refrigerant valves and lines and consolidated the high- and low-voltage controllers, reducing parts and complexity. Its modular design makes its production 80% automated and its operation 38% more efficient than other automotive thermal systems."

Proper Props

While the attendees & patrons were filing into the Launch Event, hours before the start time, Jaan @theevuniverse & Simon @residentsponge from EVWire already had the Inside Scope. Jaan put out an 8 part X thread breaking down all of the latest NEWS 1st!

Jaan & Simon from EVwire are a Must Follow, they cover All EV from ALL angles for the entire industry, 1st to the news & Setting the Standard.

Safety and federal compliance, straight from Tesla's own filing

Tesla publishes a formal compliance guide for Cybercab covering how the vehicle meets Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards despite having no steering wheel or pedals — the exact regulatory territory NHTSA has been actively rewriting rules around this year.

Read the full compliance guide (PDF) →

Tesla is already signing up fleet operators

Beyond individual riders, Tesla is actively building out a network of fleet operators and partners to scale the Robotaxi service. If you're exploring what it takes to operate or invest in a Cybercab fleet, Tesla has an official interest form live now.

Register fleet interest with Tesla →

What actually happens during a ride

After your ride ends, Tesla uses the interior cabin camera to confirm the Cybercab is ready for its next passenger, checking whether the cabin is clean and whether anything was left behind. A green light turns on any time the camera is actively recording, so you always know when it's on. Riders can also adjust interior ambient lighting colors directly from the Tesla app — @TheEvUniverse — EVWire

Photo: Jaan @ EVWire

Photo: Jaan @ EVWire

Eight cameras, and seatbelts that talk to you

Cybercab is covered by eight external and internal cameras feeding its self-driving and cabin-monitoring systems continuously.

The motorized seatbelts do more than tighten automatically. They can pulse or vibrate to get a passenger's attention, and they proactively tighten the moment the car anticipates or detects harsh braking, loss of traction, or another sudden road event.

⚠ Important: don't ride with your feet up on the dash. Airbag deployment paths assume feet are on the floor.

Not yet built for young kids

Children under 13 are not currently permitted in a Cybercab — even accompanied by an adult. Expect this to be one of the more actively revisited restrictions as Tesla expands the service.

Built with accessibility in mind, down to the door panel

Braille appears throughout the Cybercab cabin, including on interior touch points and controls — spelling out "CYBERCAB" here the same way it's marked in the car. For riders who are blind or have low vision, and for passengers with a range of physical disabilities, this is one of the small but deliberate details that make an unsupervised, driverless ride feel usable rather than just automated.

常见问题

Is Cybercab available to the public in Austin right now?

Yes, in a limited service area following the September 3, 2026 launch event. It's rolling out alongside Tesla's existing Model Y Robotaxi fleet, not replacing it yet.

Does Cybercab really have no steering wheel or pedals?

Correct — no manual controls of any kind. It's built exclusively for unsupervised autonomous operation.

What's the real range — 418 miles or 300?

418 miles is the EPA-equivalent all-electric rating (375 highway). Tesla has publicly cited approximately 300 miles as the more realistic real-world figure.

Is $0.20 per mile what I'll actually pay today?

No — that's Tesla's long-term operating-cost target once the fleet scales, not a current fare. Actual day-one pricing is tracked on our /prices page.

How is Cybercab different from the Model Y Robotaxi already running in Austin?

Same app, same service — different vehicle. Model Y Robotaxi is a standard production Model Y running Tesla's autonomy stack. Cybercab is purpose-built from the ground up with no manual controls at all.

Can Cybercab carry two people and luggage?

It's a two-seat vehicle with a front trunk for storage. It is not designed for wheelchair accessibility in its current configuration.
